newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish economy hamstrung by election prospect.
newsitem.headline: Turkish economy hamstrung by election prospect.

text.p: Turkey's government will struggle to keep the inflation-ridden economy on track and has little time to tackle structural weaknesses ahead of expected early elections, economists said on Monday.

The two-week-old coalition, fresh from a weekend confidence-vote triumph, has little room to manoeuvre between serious financial imbalances and an electorate impatient after months of political chaos.
"They have to remain populist and by doing so they lose on the fiscal side when there are elections on the horizon," said Atilla Yesilada, director of research at Global Securities.

One of the government's first measures was a 35-percent wage rise for civil servants, described by Yesilada as "excessive". He forecast the budget deficit would overshoot targets and will have to be financed by further borrowing.
The secularist coalition has already painted a gloomy picture of the economy inherited from the previous Islamist-led coalition, reinforcing fears about chronic inflation and gaping deficits.
Annual inflation of just under 80 percent is compounded by a budget deficit expected to leap to 2,400 trillion lira ($15.9 billion) in 1997 despite Islamist promises of a balanced budget.
The government's stated aim of 'fine-tuning' the economy has raised concerns among economists that it will shelve urgently needed structural reforms as previous coalitions have done.

In a televised address on Sunday night, secularist Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz poured cold water on any hopes of a quick economic fix, vowing to steer clear of populism ahead of polls likely to be held by the middle of next year.
"Nobody should expect from us populist practices, election-oriented economists or such erroneous actions. Our primary goal is to prevent devastation in the economy," he said.
Yilmaz focused on the "vicious circle of inflation" as one of the major obstacles holding the economy back, deterring investment and exacerbating unemployment.

Financial markets, which have welcomed the coalition under free-marketeer Yilmaz, are expected to look favourably on the government even if reforms remain neglected, said Izzettin Onder, professor of finance at Istanbul University.
"The new government will encourage the markets and capital and accelerate privatisation, but will not do much to correct income disparities and regional imbalances," he said.
Prices on the Istanbul Stock Exchange rose slightly in morning trade on Monday, after steady gains since the new government was formed on June 30.
The government has pledged to refrain from foreign exchange or interest rate intervention and to tighten tax collection while raising $4 billion from selloffs in 1997.
It inherits an economy likely to grow 5.5 to 6 percent in 1997.
Economists say the leftist presence in the minority alliance casts doubt on the likelihood of potentially painful structural changes, sought by the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
And a second leftist party has made its crucial support from outside the coalition contingent on early polls. Elections would normally be held in the year 2000.

"It is clear that the chances are very slim of a government supported by the left supporting structural measures proposed by the IMF rapporteurs," said Mustafa Mutlu in an editorial in the economic daily Liberal Bakis. "But the bleeding wound must be staunched."
Mutlu pointed to a current account deficit expected to reach $4-4.5 billion in 1997, domestic debt of 4,213 trillion lira and the gradual collapse of the costly social security system.

Global's Yesilada said a key government aim was to spark a merger of the centre-right in Turkey, drawing MPs from the True Path Party (DYP) of Yilmaz's bitter rival Tansu Ciller. Two DYP deputies quit the party on Monday.
Such a move would strengthen the alliance, he said.
"A major increase in its lifespan may allow it to initiate some reform, but unless this objective is achieved their ability to act is limited," he said.
($1 = 152,800 Turkish lira)
